name: CAMELS-US
description: Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies for 671 catchments in the contiguous United States.
temporalResolution: Daily meteorological and streamflow time series
limitations: Catchments are largely minimally impacted; users should review forcing-product differences.

name: Caravan
description: A community dataset of meteorological forcing, streamflow, and catchment attributes harmonized across multiple regions.
limitations: Source archives differ in record length, quality control, and streamflow availability.

name: GRDC
description: The Global Runoff Data Centre archive provides quality-controlled river discharge data contributed by national hydrological services.
provider: Global Runoff Data Centre, Federal Institute of Hydrology
temporalResolution: Daily and monthly, depending on station
limitations: Station availability, record length, and redistribution conditions vary.

name: USGS Water Data for the Nation
description: Current and historical U.S. water observations, including streamflow, groundwater levels, water quality, and site information.
temporalResolution: Instantaneous to annual, depending on site and parameter
limitations: Record completeness, approved status, and available parameters vary by station.

name: Daymet
description: Gridded estimates of daily weather parameters derived from ground observations and terrain information.
provider: NASA Oak Ridge National Laboratory Distributed Active Archive Center
spatialCoverage: North America, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico
limitations: Interpolation uncertainty varies with station density, terrain, variable, and location.

name: NLDAS
description: The North American Land Data Assimilation System combines observation-based forcing with land-surface models.
provider: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and partners
spatialCoverage: Contiguous United States and surrounding regions
limitations: Users must account for product version, forcing source, and land-model differences.

name: SMAP
description: NASA satellite observations and derived products focused on global soil moisture and freeze-thaw state.
temporalResolution: Product dependent; approximately 2–3 day global revisit
limitations: Retrieval quality is affected by vegetation, surface water, frozen ground, and radio-frequency interference.

name: GRACE and GRACE-FO
description: Satellite gravity missions used to estimate changes in terrestrial water storage at regional to global scales.
provider: NASA and German Research Centre for Geosciences
limitations: Coarse effective resolution, leakage, filtering, and mission gaps require careful treatment.

name: SWOT
description: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography mission maps water-surface elevation and extent for oceans and inland waters.
provider: NASA and Centre National d'Études Spatiales with international partners
limitations: Sampling geometry, water-body size, vegetation, and product maturity affect use.

name: SWOT River Database (SWORD)
description: A versioned, topologically consistent global river network of reaches and nodes that provides the prior framework and hydrologic and morphological attributes for SWOT river vector products and large-scale river analysis.
provider: SWORD project, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, The Ohio State University, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and collaborators
spatialResolution: Approximately 10 km reaches and 200 m nodes; coverage and variables are version dependent
useCases: SWOT RiverSP product matching and interpretation
River routing and hydrologic model integration
limitations: Match the SWORD release named in the target SWOT RiverSP product documentation.
Use v17b when reproducing SWOT Version D RiverSP workflows; v17c is a newer community release and is not the Version D JPL product baseline.
Record the selected SWORD version in reproducible workflows because topology, attributes, and product compatibility can change between releases.

name: SWOT Prior Lake Database - Scientific
description: A global inventory of lakes and reservoirs with polygon geometries and metadata, generated by combining global and regional hydrographic databases into a congruent prior dataset for SWOT lake observations and storage-change analysis.
provider: Centre National des Etudes Spatiales (CNES), Theia Data and Services Centre, and University of California, Los Angeles
spatialCoverage: Global, organized into nine continental groups and hydrographic basins
useCases: Linking SWOT lake observations through time
limitations: The Scientific collection is distributed as 71 SQLite tiles; users should choose the Light or Geometries collection when a reduced or simplified product is more appropriate.
The database is a prior hydrographic inventory and should be checked against the target SWOT product version and lake-processing workflow.
Review the ETALAB 2.0 license and the source datasets contributing to the compiled product.

name: HBV
description: A conceptual catchment hydrology model family representing snow, soil moisture, runoff generation, and routing.
provider: Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute and research community
limitations: Equations, parameters, and licensing differ across HBV implementations.

name: LSTM Rainfall–Runoff Modeling
description: Long short-term memory neural networks applied to hydrological time series and rainfall–runoff prediction.
spatialCoverage: Site, catchment, regional, or large-sample applications
limitations: Performance depends on training coverage; extrapolation, physical consistency, and interpretability need evaluation.

name: generic_deltamodel
description: A PyTorch framework for coupling neural networks with process-based equations in differentiable models.
limitations: Users must design and validate application-specific process equations, inputs, and objectives.

name: Prediction in Ungauged Basins
description: The challenge of producing reliable hydrological predictions where direct streamflow observations are unavailable.
provider: International Association of Hydrological Sciences and research community
limitations: Definitions, data availability, and evaluation protocols differ across studies and regions.

name: HYDRUS
description: A family of numerical models for simulating water, heat, and solute movement in variably saturated porous media.
limitations: Model setup, parameterization, dimensionality, and licensing vary by HYDRUS product.

name: MODFLOW 6
description: The current core version of the USGS modular hydrologic model for groundwater flow and coupled process simulations.
limitations: Results depend on conceptualization, discretization, boundary conditions, and calibration data.

name: W3RA
description: A grid-based landscape water-balance model developed for continental water-resources assessment.
limitations: Implementation access, forcing, parameter regionalization, and grid scale must be checked for each application.

name: RAPID
description: Routing Application for Parallel computatIon of Discharge, a matrix-based river-network routing model.
limitations: Network topology, runoff inputs, routing assumptions, and calibration strongly affect performance.

name: δHBV
description: A differentiable HBV-family model whose process parameters can be learned across basins with neural networks.
limitations: Results depend on the selected HBV formulation, forcings, training regions, and objective functions.

name: Soil Water Balance Modeling
description: Accounting methods that represent changes in soil-water storage from precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, and drainage.
limitations: Closure depends on input quality, storage depth, process simplification, and parameter calibration.

name: Multiscale Parameter Regionalization
description: A framework that derives model parameters from high-resolution geophysical attributes before upscaling to a model grid.
limitations: Transfer functions and upscaling operators remain model-, variable-, and scale-dependent.

name: STL Decomposition
description: Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS separates a time series into seasonal, trend, and remainder components.
limitations: Requires choices for seasonal and trend smoothing and does not replace process attribution.

name: Principal Component Analysis
description: A linear transformation that represents correlated variables with orthogonal components ordered by explained variance.
limitations: Components are linear, scale sensitive, and may not map directly to physical processes.

name: Independent Component Analysis
description: A statistical approach for separating observed multivariate signals into approximately independent latent components.
limitations: Results depend on independence assumptions, preprocessing, component count, and algorithm initialization.

name: Artificial Neural Networks
description: Layered computational models that learn nonlinear mappings from examples through parameter optimization.
limitations: Data coverage, architecture, regularization, reproducibility, and extrapolation require careful evaluation.

name: Random Forest
description: An ensemble method that combines many randomized decision trees for prediction or classification.
limitations: Feature importance can be misleading; extrapolation and spatial dependence require explicit testing.

name: Convolutional Neural Networks
description: Neural networks using shared convolutional filters to learn local and hierarchical patterns in gridded or image-like data.
limitations: Boundary treatment, receptive field, scale transfer, and data requirements influence hydrological validity.

name: Cosmic-Ray Neutron Sensing
description: A non-invasive method that infers area-average near-surface soil moisture from above-ground cosmic-ray neutron intensity.
limitations: Requires correction and calibration for atmospheric pressure, humidity, biomass, and local hydrogen pools.

name: Differentiable Programming
description: A modeling approach that composes differentiable operations so gradients can optimize parameters through entire computational systems.
limitations: Gradient stability, differentiable approximations, computational cost, and equifinality need explicit analysis.

name: Surrogate-Based Modeling
description: Statistical or machine-learning approximations of expensive process models used to accelerate analysis and optimization.
limitations: Validity is limited by training design and the sampled parameter and forcing domain.

name: Google Earth Engine
description: A cloud geospatial processing service with a public data catalog, compute infrastructure, APIs, and an interactive code editor.
limitations: Quotas, licensing, dataset-specific caveats, and server-side programming patterns must be considered.

name: ArcGIS Pro
description: A commercial desktop GIS for mapping, spatial analysis, data management, and geoprocessing workflows.
limitations: Requires an appropriate license; tool availability varies by extension and license level.

name: QGIS
description: An open-source geographic information system for viewing, editing, analyzing, and publishing geospatial information.
limitations: Plugin quality and workflow reproducibility vary; large analyses may require external processing tools.

name: GDAL
description: An open-source translator library and command-line toolkit for raster and vector geospatial data formats.
limitations: Driver capabilities and build dependencies vary by format and installation.

name: PyTorch
description: An open-source machine-learning framework with tensor computation, automatic differentiation, and accelerator support.
limitations: Reproducibility, numerical precision, device behavior, and rapidly evolving APIs require management.

name: TensorFlow
description: An end-to-end open-source platform for numerical computation, machine-learning model development, training, and deployment.
limitations: Version compatibility, hardware configuration, and deployment targets add workflow complexity.

name: scikit-learn
description: An open-source Python library for supervised and unsupervised learning, preprocessing, model selection, and evaluation.
limitations: Most estimators do not directly model spatial or temporal dependence; users must design validation accordingly.

name: International Soil Moisture Network
description: A global data-hosting facility for harmonized, quality-controlled in situ soil-moisture and accompanying variables.
provider: International Centre for Water Resources and Global Change and Federal Institute of Hydrology
limitations: Network density, sensor type, depth, record length, and temporal sampling are heterogeneous.

name: GLDAS
description: The Global Land Data Assimilation System combines satellite and ground observations with land-surface models to produce global fields.
limitations: Model structure, forcing, assimilation, version, and variable definition affect interpretation.

name: CPC Global Unified Daily Precipitation
description: A global daily gauge-based precipitation analysis produced through the NOAA Climate Prediction Center unified precipitation project.
provider: NOAA Climate Prediction Center and Physical Sciences Laboratory
limitations: Gauge density varies; real-time values may change and some source dates are missing.

name: MODIS Land Products
description: A family of Terra and Aqua Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer products for surface reflectance, land-surface temperature, land cover, vegetation indices, evapotranspiration, snow, water masks, fires, and related Earth-observation variables.
provider: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and MODIS science teams
limitations: Clouds, retrieval algorithms, quality flags, composite periods, and collection versions must be handled per product.
Terra and Aqua overpass timing and product availability differ among collections.
Spatial and temporal resolution, uncertainty, and quality screening are product dependent; users should use the relevant QA fields.
Individual MODIS products are not interchangeable and may require atmospheric correction, compositing, or scale-factor handling.

name: NOAA Climate Data Online
description: A discovery and access service for historical weather and climate datasets held by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information.
provider: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
limitations: Coverage, quality flags, station continuity, and access interfaces vary among datasets.

name: SoilGrids
description: Global maps of soil properties at standard depth intervals produced using machine-learning-based digital soil mapping.
limitations: Predictions carry spatially varying uncertainty and should not replace local soil observations.

name: MERIT Hydro
description: A global hydrography dataset derived from MERIT DEM that provides flow direction, hydrologically adjusted elevation, upstream area and gradient, river width, and height above nearest drainage.
provider: Global Hydrodynamics Lab, Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo
spatialResolution: 3 arc-seconds, approximately 90 m at the equator
access: Registration; dual licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 or ODbL 1.0
limitations: Version 1.0.1 uses a single D8 downstream direction; users should review known limitations for coasts, channel bifurcations, glaciers, and human-made water systems.

name: NOAA NextGen Hydrofabric
description: A cloud-native hydrologic geospatial fabric of catchments, flow paths, network topology, hydrolocations, and model attributes designed for NOAA's NextGen water-resources modeling framework.
provider: NOAA Office of Water Prediction, USGS, and Lynker
spatialResolution: Catchment and flow-path features; NextGen target catchments are generally 3–10 km²
limitations: Artifacts are preliminary or provisional, coverage and versions vary by domain, and ODbL attribution and share-alike conditions apply to adapted databases.

name: HydroSHEDS
description: A global family of hydrographic layers derived from conditioned elevation data, including elevation, drainage direction, flow accumulation, flow length, land masks, and sinks.
spatialCoverage: Global, with product- and resolution-dependent coverage
spatialResolution: 3, 15, and 30 arc-seconds; selected products at 5 or 6 arc-minutes
access: Open under the applicable HydroSHEDS product license
limitations: Version 1 core products north of 60°N rely on coarser HYDRO1k data and are not available there at the highest 3 arc-second resolution; users must check product-specific licenses.

name: NHDPlus High Resolution
description: A high-resolution U.S. hydrography framework combining detailed stream networks, watershed boundaries, elevation-derived catchments, flow connectivity, and value-added hydrologic attributes.
spatialCoverage: Conterminous United States, Hawaii, parts of Alaska, and selected U.S. territories
temporalResolution: Static, versioned by vector processing unit
spatialResolution: Based on 1:24,000-scale or more detailed hydrography and 10 m elevation data
limitations: Availability and versions vary by region; vector geodatabases and raster components are distributed as separate, potentially large archives.

name: National Water Prediction Service (NWPS)
description: NOAA's national interactive service for current river observations, official NWS streamflow forecasts, National Water Model guidance, flood impacts, and related hydrologic information.
provider: NOAA National Weather Service Office of Water Prediction
temporalResolution: Current observations and forecast products, source dependent
spatialResolution: Gauges, reaches, and mapped national products
limitations: Some layers and services are experimental, availability varies by product, and the service is not a complete historical archive.

name: USGS Water Cycle
description: A plain-language USGS overview of where water is stored in the atmosphere, on land, and underground; how it moves; and how natural processes and human activities affect the water cycle.
provider: U.S. Geological Survey Water Science School
useCases: Conceptual framing of water stores and fluxes
limitations: This is an educational reference, not a dataset, numerical model, operational monitoring service, or forecast product.

name: Hydrography Resource Selection Guide
description: A practical guide for distinguishing SWORD, MERIT Hydro, NHDPlus High Resolution, NOAA NextGen Hydrofabric, and HydroSHEDS when choosing a hydrography resource for hydrological research.
spatialCoverage: Global and United States, depending on the selected resource
temporalResolution: Static and versioned products; guide updated with catalog metadata
spatialResolution: Dataset dependent, from global grids and river reaches to high-resolution catchments and flowpaths
useCases: Choose SWORD for SWOT river observation, RiverSP product matching, and global river reaches and nodes
Choose MERIT Hydro for global DEM-derived drainage direction, flow accumulation, terrain attributes, and large-scale routing
Choose HydroSHEDS for global multi-resolution hydrography, watershed delineation, and basin-scale analysis
Choose NHDPlus High Resolution for detailed United States hydrography, catchments, flow connectivity, and value-added routing attributes
Choose NOAA NextGen Hydrofabric for model-ready United States catchments, flowpaths, hydrolocations, cloud-native artifacts, and NOAA NextGen domains
limitations: Check product version, spatial support, topology, licensing, and geographic coverage before use.
Match SWORD releases to the target SWOT RiverSP product and record the selected version in reproducible workflows.
Confirm that the selected resource's representation and attributes are compatible with the target hydrological model, routing scheme, or satellite product.

name: Human-influenced Hydrological Prediction
description: The challenge of predicting hydrological states and fluxes when reservoir operations, water withdrawals, irrigation, land-use change, urbanization, and adaptive human behavior alter natural processes and create two-way human–water feedbacks.
provider: International Association of Hydrological Sciences Panta Rhei initiative and research community
spatialCoverage: Global, with emphasis on managed and rapidly changing water systems
spatialResolution: Managed sites and catchments to regional and global human–water systems
useCases: Attribution of natural and human drivers
limitations: Human decisions, infrastructure, and water-use data are often incomplete; adaptive behavior, causality, nonstationarity, and uncertainty remain difficult to represent and evaluate.

name: Cross-scale Hydrological Simulation
description: The challenge of reconciling observations, processes, states, parameters, and model representations across spatial supports from points to the globe and temporal scales from individual events to long-term change.
temporalResolution: Event, seasonal, interannual, and long-term scales
spatialResolution: Points and plots to grids, catchments, regions, and global domains
limitations: Scale-dependent processes and parameters may not transfer directly; heterogeneity and aggregation can remove information, while fine-resolution simulation increases computational, calibration, and uncertainty-analysis costs.

name: OpenET Evapotranspiration Data
description: A satellite-based evapotranspiration data service providing ensemble and model-specific estimates through Google Earth Engine, Data Explorer, APIs, and raster or geodatabase services.
spatialCoverage: United States; collection and service dependent
temporalResolution: Daily archive from approximately 2016 and monthly records from approximately 2000, model dependent
spatialResolution: Approximately 30 m Landsat-scale grids; aggregation depends on the API or service
access: Open; account or API registration and service-specific quotas may apply
limitations: Ensemble, model, collection version, variables, and temporal coverage differ across products.
OpenET is primarily United States focused and should not be assumed globally complete.
Recent estimates may be revised as satellite inputs and model implementations are updated.
API and Earth Engine access may require registration, credentials, or quotas.
Large requests may require spatial or temporal tiling.
Record the selected model or ensemble, collection version, date range, and access route for reproducibility.

name: ESA CCI Soil Moisture
description: A global daily surface-soil-moisture climate data record generated from merged active-microwave, passive-microwave, and combined satellite products, with versioned annual releases and supporting documentation.
provider: ESA Climate Change Initiative Soil Moisture project and consortium partners
temporalResolution: Daily; product-dependent time spans, with current v09.2 extending through 31 December 2024
access: Open; free CEDA downloads, with version- and archive-specific terms
useCases: Global soil-moisture monitoring and anomaly analysis
Hydrological model initialization and data assimilation
limitations: ACTIVE, PASSIVE, and COMBINED products have different sensors, units, uncertainty characteristics, and temporal coverage.
ACTIVE soil moisture is expressed as saturation percentage, while PASSIVE and COMBINED products use volumetric units; these must not be mixed without conversion.
The product represents near-surface soil moisture, approximately the upper 2–5 cm, rather than root-zone storage.
Retrieval quality and coverage are degraded or unavailable under snow, ice, frozen soil, dense vegetation, surface water, urban areas, and complex terrain.
The approximately 25 km grid is too coarse for field-scale management or local sensor replacement.
Sensor inputs, algorithms, rescaling, and uncertainty treatment change across releases; workflows must record the product family and exact version.
Redistribution and usage conditions should be checked for the selected archive and version.

name: SWAT / SWAT+ (Soil & Water Assessment Tool)
description: A watershed- and river-basin-scale ecohydrological model family for simulating water quantity and quality, sediment, nutrients, vegetation, and land-management or climate impacts; SWAT+ is the current restructured model.
provider: SWAT development community, USDA Agricultural Research Service, and Texas A&M AgriLife Research
spatialCoverage: Small watersheds to large river basins; regional and continental applications
temporalResolution: Typically daily; configuration and input dependent
spatialResolution: Subbasin and hydrologic response unit (HRU) based; setup dependent
access: Open; SWAT+ and legacy SWAT distributions, interfaces, and documentation
useCases: Sediment, nutrient, and nonpoint-source pollution studies
limitations: SWAT and SWAT+ require diverse topographic, soil, land-use, meteorological, and management inputs.
Results depend on watershed delineation, hydrologic response unit configuration, parameterization, forcing quality, and calibration.
SWAT and SWAT+ use substantially different input organization and spatial representations; record the model generation, release, interface, and setup.
Semi-distributed abstractions may not resolve local groundwater, channel, or management processes without additional coupling or refinement.

name: ParFlow
description: A parallel, integrated hydrology model that couples three-dimensional saturated and variably saturated subsurface flow with overland flow and land-surface processes such as evapotranspiration and snow.
provider: ParFlow development community and partner institutions
spatialCoverage: Catchment to continental domains; application dependent
spatialResolution: Three-dimensional orthogonal or terrain-following mesh; domain and application dependent
access: Open; source releases and documentation are publicly available under the project license
useCases: Integrated groundwater and surface-water flow simulation
Variably saturated vadose-zone and subsurface transport studies
Land-surface, evapotranspiration, snow, and energy-balance coupling
High-resolution watershed and continental simulations on parallel computers
Hydrologic forecasting, data assimilation, and climate-impact analysis
limitations: Three-dimensional distributed simulations can require substantial parameter, forcing, storage, and high-performance-computing resources.
Results are sensitive to hydraulic properties, discretization, initial and boundary conditions, forcing, and coupling choices.
Capabilities and input compatibility vary by ParFlow release, build, solver configuration, and optional CLM coupling.
Model setup requires careful numerical, parallel-computing, and surface-subsurface conceptualization decisions; report the exact release and configuration.

name: Groundwater Sustainability in Intensively Irrigated Agricultural Plains
description: The challenge of sustaining groundwater-dependent agriculture in large irrigated plains while pumping, recharge, crop water demand, climate variability, water quality, and management decisions interact across heterogeneous aquifers and administrative boundaries. The North China Plain is shaped by monsoon-seasonal water supply and winter-wheat–summer-maize irrigation; the U.S. High Plains is shaped by semiarid recharge variability, aquifer heterogeneity, groundwater–stream connectivity, and state/local governance. They are useful comparison cases, not interchangeable hydrogeologic systems.
provider: Hydrological modeling and water-resources research community
spatialCoverage: North China Plain, China, and High Plains aquifer region, United States; transferable to other irrigated alluvial plains
temporalResolution: Seasonal to multidecadal; event and operational scales for irrigation and recharge
spatialResolution: Field and well scales to aquifer, basin, and regional scales
access: Open literature and public monitoring/model data
useCases: Comparative groundwater-budget and depletion assessment across the NCP and HPA
Irrigation timing, crop adaptation, evapotranspiration, and water-productivity analysis
Conjunctive surface-water and groundwater management and recharge assessment
Groundwater–stream interaction and baseflow impact assessment
Drought, climate-change, recharge, and pumping scenario analysis
Cross-region model transfer, data assimilation, and uncertainty evaluation
limitations: The two regions differ in aquifer architecture, recharge regime, crop calendars, data density, and institutions; comparative results require harmonized definitions and cannot assume parameter transfer.
Groundwater withdrawals, irrigation volumes, well locations, crop water use, and water-quality observations may be incomplete or inconsistent across scales.
Remote-sensing products constrain storage, soil moisture, or evapotranspiration indirectly and do not replace local well and pumping observations.
Aquifer depletion, streamflow impacts, and water-quality responses can have long lags; short evaluation periods may misrepresent sustainability.
Model results depend on conceptualization, boundary conditions, recharge and return-flow estimates, pumping records, calibration targets, and scenario assumptions.
Water-saving technology may reduce applied water without proportional reductions in consumptive use or basin-scale depletion; water budgets and rebound effects must be evaluated.

name: MSWEP / MSWX Global Climate Forcing
description: A complementary family of global climate-forcing products from GloH2O: MSWEP provides gauge-, satellite-, and reanalysis-based precipitation estimates, while MSWX provides bias-corrected near-surface meteorological variables across historical, near-real-time, and forecast products. They can be used together, but they are not interchangeable and must be selected by variable, version, temporal product, and modeling objective.
spatialCoverage: Global; MSWEP includes land and ocean coverage, while MSWX focuses on global land meteorology
temporalResolution: Product dependent: hourly or 3-hourly historical/near-real-time forcing, with MSWX 10-day and 7-month forecast products
spatialResolution: Approximately 0.1° for current products; original MSWEP releases used 0.25°
access: Non-commercial access by request under CC BY-NC 4.0; commercial access and API terms differ
useCases: Global rainfall-runoff and hydrological model forcing
Global precipitation and meteorological product comparison
Medium-range and seasonal forecast ensemble experiments
limitations: MSWEP and MSWX provide different variable sets and should not be treated as one homogeneous dataset.
MSWEP versions and variants differ in gauge corrections, temporal resolution, latency, and input sources.
MSWX-Past, MSWX-NRT, MSWX-Mid, and MSWX-Long differ in forcing systems, forecast horizons, uncertainty, and availability.
Gauge density, satellite retrieval quality, reanalysis skill, and bias-correction performance vary by region and season.
Bias correction and downscaling may alter local distributions or physical relationships among variables; local validation remains necessary.
The 0.1° grid does not resolve field-scale variability, convective precipitation structure, or complex terrain.
Users must record whether they used MSWEP or MSWX, the exact version/subproduct, variables, temporal aggregation, forecast lead time, access route, and license terms.

name: USGS HYDRoSWOT Hydroacoustic Dataset
description: A USGS hydroacoustic dataset supporting the SWOT mission by aggregating acoustic Doppler current profiler measurements from the USGS streamgaging network, including channel geometry, discharge, stage, velocity, depth, width, and station metadata.
provider: U.S. Geological Survey Colorado Water Science Center
spatialCoverage: United States; more than 5,000 streamgage stations
temporalResolution: Irregular measurement events; station and measurement dependent
useCases: In situ river discharge and channel-geometry analysis
Machine-learning estimation of river width, depth, velocity, or discharge
Comparison of satellite observations with field measurements
limitations: Coverage is limited to the United States and should not be interpreted as a global HYDRoSWOT product.
The release contains ADCP measurements only; other discharge-measurement methods are not represented.
Measurements are irregular in time and may not describe continuous daily or sub-daily conditions.
Station observations represent local cross-sections and may not represent reach-scale or basin-scale behavior.
Measurement quality, channel conditions, and metadata completeness vary among stations and visits.
Users should record the data-release version, station identifiers, measurement dates, quality controls, and any aggregation applied.

name: Global Dam Watch (GDW) Consensus Database
description: A versioned global database of river barriers and associated reservoirs that integrates, harmonizes, and quality-controls multiple dam and obstruction datasets, co-registering features with HydroSHEDS and RiverATLAS for large-scale hydrological and environmental analysis.
temporalResolution: Static, versioned releases; construction dates and reservoir observations are attribute dependent
spatialResolution: Barrier points and reservoir polygons; v1.0 features are co-registered to a 15-arc-second HydroSHEDS drainage grid
access: Open under CC BY 4.0; downloads and visualisation available through Global Dam Watch and Figshare
useCases: Global dam, river-barrier, and reservoir inventories
Reservoir storage, surface-area, and water-management studies
Hydrological model parameterization and human-impact assessment
Hydropower, irrigation, flood-control, and environmental-flow analysis
Cross-basin and global comparison of artificial surface-water infrastructure
limitations: GDW v1.0 is a harmonized consensus product, not a guaranteed complete inventory of every small barrier or reservoir.
Version 1.0 prioritizes larger dams, reservoirs, and barriers on larger rivers; small structures may be underrepresented.
Source datasets differ in detection method, spatial completeness, attribute definitions, and regional bias.
Reservoir polygons may reflect seasonal or source-specific water extents rather than maximum operational storage.
Construction dates, storage capacity, purpose, and other attributes may be missing, estimated, or uncertain.
Users should check the exact GDW release, source provenance, duplicate handling, spatial support, and CC BY attribution requirements.

name: Foundation Models for Hydrology
description: A machine-learning paradigm in which a large model is pretrained on broad, heterogeneous data and adapted to multiple downstream hydrological tasks through fine-tuning, prompting, or zero-shot inference. Hydrological applications include rainfall-runoff prediction, streamflow forecasting, soil-moisture and evapotranspiration estimation, remote-sensing interpretation, and regional transfer, with explicit attention to spatial and temporal support, physical constraints, uncertainty, and domain shift.
spatialCoverage: Application dependent; potentially global when trained on multi-region Earth-system data
temporalResolution: Application and pretraining-corpus dependent; event to multidecadal
spatialResolution: Application dependent; station, catchment, grid, reach, or pixel
access: Open literature; implementation, pretrained weights, and training data are model dependent
useCases: Cross-basin pretraining for rainfall-runoff and streamflow forecasting
Zero-shot or few-shot transfer to ungauged and data-scarce basins
Multi-task prediction of streamflow, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, water quality, and remote-sensing variables
Spatiotemporal representation learning from heterogeneous forcings and static attributes
Fine-tuning Earth-system foundation backbones for hydrological prediction
Hybrid, physics-aware, or surrogate-model coupling experiments
limitations: Foundation models are a paradigm rather than a standardized product; architectures, training data, objectives, checkpoints, and licenses differ.
Spatial and temporal leakage, station overlap, and benchmark contamination require strict evaluation splits.
Domain shift, climate nonstationarity, sparse observations, and negative transfer can limit regional generalization.
Learned predictions do not automatically satisfy water balance, conservation, or other physical constraints.
Extreme events, uncertainty calibration, out-of-distribution behavior, and causal interpretation require separate evaluation.
Pretraining can require substantial compute, storage, energy, and specialized infrastructure.
Reproducible workflows must record the model name, checkpoint, training corpus, variables, spatial and temporal support, fine-tuning data, software version, and license.
